questions.question: What is an independent variable in an experiment?
choices: A factor deliberately changed by the investigator
The outcome being measured
A factor kept constant
An error in a measuring instrument

questions.question: What is a dependent variable?
choices: A factor deliberately held constant
The outcome measured in response to a change
The name of the experimental group
A prediction written before testing

questions.question: What is a controlled variable?
choices: An outcome that must increase
A treatment given only to one group
A factor kept consistent across comparison groups
A measurement removed from the results

questions.question: What is the purpose of a control group?
choices: To receive every possible treatment at once
To guarantee the expected result
To replace measurements with predictions
To provide a comparison for evaluating a treatment

questions.question: What is a repeated trial?
choices: A summary of someone else's conclusion
A change in all experimental variables
Another run of a test under the same planned conditions
A prediction made after deleting data

questions.question: What is a confounding variable?
choices: An additional factor that makes the treatment's effect difficult to separate
A factor that is perfectly controlled
The numerical unit used in a graph
A measurement that agrees with a hypothesis

questions.question: What does random assignment mean?
choices: Choosing only volunteers who expect success
Using chance to place participants or subjects into treatment groups
Assigning groups by alphabetical order
Giving every group the same treatment

questions.question: Why should comparison groups be similar before a treatment begins?
choices: Similar groups eliminate all measurement uncertainty
Differences should be introduced after the results are known
Only identical outcomes can be compared
Initial differences could otherwise explain the results

questions.question: Why is changing one main variable at a time often helpful?
choices: It makes repeated trials unnecessary
It prevents all variation among subjects
It makes the effect of that variable easier to interpret
It ensures the hypothesis is supported

questions.question: Why can more repeated trials improve an investigation?
choices: They help reveal variation and reduce the influence of unusual results
They remove the need for a control group
They guarantee every measurement is identical
They allow researchers to select only favorable results

questions.question: How does random sampling differ from random assignment?
choices: Sampling applies treatments; assignment selects measuring units
They always mean exactly the same thing
Sampling eliminates all bias; assignment eliminates all uncertainty
Sampling selects subjects from a population; assignment places them in study groups

questions.question: Why should investigators decide how to measure an outcome before collecting data?
choices: It makes actual measurements optional
It promotes consistent measurements and reduces selective interpretation
It allows the outcome to be changed whenever results disagree
It ensures that no unexpected result occurs

questions.question: Why can blinding an observer improve an experiment?
choices: It allows subjects to be measured without consent
It prevents instruments from recording data
It guarantees no confounding variables exist
Knowing the treatment can unintentionally influence observations

questions.question: What is a limitation of testing a treatment on only one organism?
choices: Organisms cannot be measured
A single organism always represents its species perfectly
Individual differences may be mistaken for a treatment effect
Control groups are useful only with large organisms

questions.question: What makes an experimental conclusion appropriately cautious?
choices: It states that the treatment works in every possible setting
It considers the tested conditions and the study's limitations
It ignores any variation in the results
It treats the original prediction as evidence

questions.question: Plants receive different fertilizer amounts, and their final heights are measured. What is the dependent variable?
choices: Final plant height
Plant species
Pot size
Fertilizer amount

questions.question: A student tests light's effect on plant growth. Which factor should be kept consistent?
choices: The amount of light being tested
The amount of water supplied
The resulting plant height
The difference between the groups' results

questions.question: A fertilizer group gets more water than a comparison group. Why is the conclusion uncertain?
choices: Water cannot affect plants
The comparison group becomes an independent variable
The fertilizer must have no effect
The effects of fertilizer and water are confounded

questions.question: A new filter is tested with muddy water. What makes a useful comparison?
choices: Compare filtered and unfiltered samples from the same starting mixture
Use clearer water for the new filter
Test untreated water from a different source only
Measure only the filter's color

questions.question: A researcher tests a material's strength using one sample, which breaks unusually early. What improvement best checks whether this result is typical?
choices: Report the result without recording the procedure
Change the strength unit after the test
Test multiple comparable samples with the same procedure
Assume all samples will break at the same point
